stops.name: La Laguna, the Battle of La Laguna
stops.campa: Fresh from a victory at Tinteros, Padilla learns of a coordinated royalist advance: two thousand men under Miguel Tacón from Chuquisaca, seven hundred under Francisco Javier de Aguilera from Vallegrande. He splits his force, ordering infantry to meet Aguilera head-on while cavalry under Cueto strikes the rear; the plan misfires when Aguilera's rearguard holds and Padilla's line falls back in disorder toward La Laguna. It is not yet the disaster it will become within a day, but the republiqueta, victorious so many times in fifteen places across this province, has never before been caught between two royalist columns at once.

stops.name: El Villar, the death and the pike
stops.campa: Padilla regroups at the sanctuary of El Villar; Aguilera, trailing him unseen, launches a surprise cavalry raid the next morning. Juana, commanding the reserve with the treasury and the arms, takes two gunshot wounds, leg and chest, and fights on through the pain to hold the line. Padilla is shot from his horse and, by the most repeated account, beheaded where he falls; Aguilera mounts his head on a pike in the plaza of El Villar, and beside it, by mistake, the head of a woman fighter he takes for Juana herself. She learns of her widowhood still bleeding, on the road, and has to be kept by her own men from riding back to die at his side.

stops.name: Valle de Segura, the treasury, Luisa, and the vow
stops.campa: Wounded and widowed within the same day, Juana does not stop to grieve where she is told the grief is safe. She rides for the Valle de Segura to secure what remains of the republiqueta's treasury, some sixty thousand duros, her one surviving daughter Luisa, and the documents that hold her own commission as teniente coronel, prizes she judges the war cannot afford to lose along with her husband. Over his unmarked grave, later, she will swear the vow her own hand records for the government: to avenge his death and to go on living by his example, whatever it costs her.
stops.quote: Only the sacred love of my country has made bearable the loss of a husband over whose grave I swore to avenge his death and follow his example.
stops.quote_source: Letter to the government, cited in Argentine historiography (El Historiador; correspondence archives, 1810s-1820s)

stops.name: La Laguna, the recovery of Padilla's head
stops.campa: Juana sends the recruiter Caipé through the villages to raise a hundred indigenous volunteers and a hundred women fighters, and leads them back against Colonel Francisco Baruri's garrison at La Laguna in what the histories of the war call its cruelest reprisal: every royalist soldier found is killed. Padilla's head, weeks on its pike, maggot-infested and picked over by crows, is taken down and brought to a church altar to be given the honors owed a colonel of the republic. It is not peace. It is the only mercy the war still has to offer a widow who buried four children before she buried, in pieces, her husband.

stops.name: La Laguna, the council of caudillos
stops.campa: With Padilla dead the republiqueta's captains gather in council and, unusually for the age, elect Juana herself to preside over the choice of his successor; she names Jacinto Cueto commander, with Esteban Fernández as his second. The unity does not hold. Apolinar Zárate and others break away, some drawn as much by the recovered treasury as by any quarrel of strategy, and the republiqueta that fought as one body under the Padillas begins to fragment into rival bands. Juana, widowed, wounded, and outranking every man in the room by commission if not by vote, watches fifteen years of shared war start to come apart in a single meeting.

stops.name: Salta, joining Martín Miguel de Güemes
stops.campa: As the republiqueta splinters behind her, Juana sends word south by the friar José Indalecio de Salazar to Martín Miguel de Güemes, the gaucho commander who has made Salta into the shield that keeps the royalists from ever again reaching Tucumán. Güemes receives her with the honor her commission is owed, appoints a successor to Padilla's command whom the local chiefs will not accept, and takes Juana herself into the irregular war he is fighting along the Salta-Jujuy frontier: the gaucho partisan bands, the same tactics of ambush and vanishing that she perfected in Chuquisaca's ravines, now practiced on the southern edge of the same war.

stops.name: The Salta-Jujuy frontier, the gaucho war
stops.campa: For three years Juana rides the borderland between Salta and Jujuy as one of Güemes's officers, part of a partisan war fought without pitched battles: ambush the royalist patrol, vanish into the quebradas, let the mountains do the work regular armies cannot. The relationship between the widowed colonel and the gaucho general grows, by the account both contemporaries and later historians credit, into something more than command and subordinate, though neither leaves a record plain enough to settle it. What is certain is that for these years she has, for the first time since Padilla's death, a war whose commander she trusts absolutely.

stops.name: Salta, the death of Güemes
stops.campa: A royalist raiding party surprises Güemes outside Salta on the night of 7 June 1821; he is shot and dies of the wound on the seventeenth, the last great guerrilla commander of the northern war gone within days of the injury. For Juana the loss closes a chapter she cannot reopen: her military career, in any effective sense, ends with his. Without Güemes's protection and without a republiqueta left whole enough to command, she is a teniente coronel and later coronel of an army that no longer has a northern front to give her, and the long decline into poverty begins here, not later.

stops.name: Chuquisaca, return and the memorial to the government
stops.campa: With the Spanish withdrawal from Upper Peru all but complete, Juana returns after nearly a decade away to a Chuquisaca now calling itself Sucre, bringing eleven-year-old Luisa and little else. No one in the city greets her; the caudillos who could vouch for her service are scattered or dead, and the new administration owes her nothing it has yet chosen to pay. She writes to the government the memorial that will define the rest of her life, asking not for charity but for what the law itself allows a widow and an officer: her husband's pension, and the salary of her own rank.
stops.quote: The enjoyment of my late husband's widow's pension, and the salary that may correspond to my own rank.
stops.quote_source: Memorial to the Bolivian government, 1825, cited in Argentine and Bolivian biographical accounts

stops.name: Chuquisaca, the visit of Bolívar and Sucre
stops.campa: In the days after Chuquisaca votes itself the capital of the republic that will bear his name, Simón Bolívar, with Antonio José de Sucre at his side, calls on Juana in person, an honor he pays almost no one else in the new state. He grants her a pension of sixty pesos, the rank of coronel, and, to the officers around him, the sentence that will outlast every honor Upper Peru gives her in her lifetime: that this country should not be called Bolivia after his own name, but Padilla or Azurduy, since it was they who made it free. Sucre will later raise the pension to a hundred pesos.

stops.name: Cullco, the hacienda restored, the letter to Manuela Sáenz
stops.campa: Of all the Azurduy and Padilla properties confiscated across fifteen years of war, the government recognizes her claim to only one, the hacienda of Cullco, which poverty will eventually force her to sell for far less than its worth. From there, on 15 December 1825, newly confirmed coronel, she writes to Manuela Sáenz, herself a colonel and Bolívar's companion, a letter of restrained feeling: gratitude for the rank, discomfort at seeing former royalist officers now serving beside the victors, and grief, plainly stated and without bitterness, for the comrades and the women fighters who did not live to see this recognition arrive.

stops.name: Sucre, the pension cut, decades of poverty
stops.campa: Bolívar's pension, already reduced by successive administrations that treat Upper Peru's war debts as someone else's to honor, is cancelled outright in 1857 under President José María Linares. Buenos Aires, for its part, has long since decided the Alto Perú campaigns are a foreign country's history and owes her nothing. Her sister Rosalía controls what family property remains; Luisa marries and moves away. Juana, alone, takes in a crippled orphan boy, Indalecio Sandi, and raises him on almost nothing, the same instinct that once made her a mother to Huallparrimachi turned now toward a stranger's child in her own old age.
